interview_metadata.name: Beulah Froneberger
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I grew up in Ringgold, Georgia, pretty much tucked between family, church potlucks, back roads, and the foothills. My family is white and working-class, and we did not have a lot extra, but there was always somebody bringing food over or fixing something in the driveway. My mom worked at a dental office for a long time, mostly front desk and insurance paperwork, and my dad has done maintenance and warehouse work around Chattanooga and northwest Georgia. I was a quiet kid, kind of dreamy and messy, always drawing in the margins of school papers or taking pictures of old barns and creek beds. My grandma quilted and my uncle did a little woodcarving, and that made handmade things feel normal to me, not fancy. In high school I started taking art more seriously after an art teacher let me stay after school and use the good paper and paints. I got interested in watercolor landscapes, analog photography, and later digital illustration on my iPad. I am 19 now, never married, no children, and I am working on an associate degree in visual arts at a community college while thinking about transferring later for illustration and museum studies. I am not in the regular workforce right now, but I pick up small freelance art things when I can, like pet portraits, event flyers, and little illustrations for people I know. I also volunteer at the local historical museum helping catalog artifacts, which made me realize I love community stories, not just making pretty pictures. I am close to my family, but I am also trying to become my own person, which has meant learning from online art spaces, reading graphic novels, and meeting people who think differently than a lot of folks I grew up around. I would not say I have had one giant dramatic life event, but graduating high school and choosing art instead of trying to jump straight into whatever job was available felt big.

follow_ups.question: What is one childhood memory that feels especially tied to who you are now?
follow_ups.response: I remember sitting on my grandma's porch with a box of colored pencils while the adults talked after Sunday lunch. I drew the same ridge line over and over, and I think that is where my love of local landscapes really started.

follow_ups.question: Who encouraged your art the most when you were younger?
follow_ups.response: My high school art teacher, Mrs. Kendall, was probably the biggest one. She treated my sketches like they were worth taking seriously, even when I was just doodling old houses and moths.

follow_ups.question: What is your family like about your art plans now?
follow_ups.response: They are supportive, but cautious. My mom tells people I am talented, then turns around and asks how I am going to afford health insurance someday.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after high school. A lot of people around me were either going straight to work, going to a bigger college if they could afford it, or staying close and taking classes. I had thought about getting a retail job full-time because money was tight and I felt guilty being an art person when everybody else was being practical. Then I helped with a small exhibit at the local historical museum, mostly labeling objects and photographing donations, and I realized I could connect art with local history. That changed something for me. I decided to enroll in community college for visual arts instead of just working, and I started taking freelance commissions seriously. It was not glamorous. I was filling out forms late at night, misplacing papers, and worrying about gas money. But it made me feel like I had a direction.

follow_ups.question: What were the options you were weighing most seriously?
follow_ups.response: Full-time retail or food service, community college for art, or trying to move farther away for school before I was ready. Community college felt like the only option that did not completely panic me.

follow_ups.question: What made the museum experience stand out?
follow_ups.response: I handled these old photos from families around Catoosa County, and they felt alive somehow. I liked that art could preserve somebody's ordinary life.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone push you one way or another?
follow_ups.response: My mom pushed stability, my art teacher pushed school, and my museum supervisor pushed me to think bigger than just commissions.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious, but not clean and confident. I remember sitting at the kitchen table with my laptop open and actually choosing visual arts on the application, like, okay, I am doing this even if it is messy.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel risky?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly financially. I knew art was not the safest route.

follow_ups.question: What helped you commit?
follow_ups.response: Seeing that community college let me stay home and keep costs lower helped a lot.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Definitely. Better advising about art careers would have helped, and honestly scholarships that are easier to understand. I had support emotionally, but I was confused about money and transfer paths.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A clear checklist for financial aid and transferring, plus somebody explaining what museum studies jobs actually look like.

follow_ups.question: Did you ask for help?
follow_ups.response: A little, but I get embarrassed when I do not know basic things, so sometimes I just Googled it at midnight.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner and I do not have children. The main people are my mom, dad, younger brother, and my grandmother on my mom's side. My mom, Denise, is the person I talk to most day-to-day, even when we annoy each other. She is practical and keeps lists, and I am the opposite, so she is always reminding me about appointments and deadlines. My dad, Carl, is quieter and shows care by fixing my car or asking if I need gas money. My younger brother Eli is 15, and we mostly joke around, send each other dumb videos, and sometimes I help him with school art projects. My grandma Ruth lives nearby and still cooks big Sunday meals when she feels up to it. She is the one who taught me to look at fabric patterns and old family objects as stories. Family can feel close and nosy at the same time here, but I do depend on them.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your grandmother?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week, often Sunday afternoon, and sometimes I stop by after class if Mom needs me to drop something off.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your brother do together?
follow_ups.response: We watch movies, play casual video games, and sometimes hike shorter trails if I bribe him with snacks.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating anyone casually?
follow_ups.response: No, not really. I have had crushes and a couple almost-things, but right now school and art take up most of my attention.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have an aunt, Melissa, who lives in Fort Oglethorpe, and we see her at birthdays and holidays. We are friendly, but not super close.

follow_ups.question: Do you have cousins nearby?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a couple, but we mostly keep up through family gatherings and Instagram.

follow_ups.question: Any family conflict that shapes things?
follow_ups.response: Nothing huge, just normal money stress and people having opinions.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friend is Kenzie, who I met in high school art class. We get coffee in Ringgold or Chattanooga and send each other half-finished drawings. I also have a friend named Mara from community college who is into photography, and we sometimes do film-development nights in my bathroom-darkroom setup. Through the Ringgold Trails Club I know a few older adults who hike on Saturdays, and they are not best friends exactly, but they are kind and steady. At the museum, my supervisor, Mr. Haney, has been important because he trusts me with real cataloging work.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Kenzie?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week or every other week, depending on classes and her work schedule.

follow_ups.question: What do your small gatherings look like?
follow_ups.response: Usually coffee, board games, sketching, or sitting on somebody's floor talking while music plays.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Ringgold, in a pretty quiet area with older houses, yards, churches, and people who know whose truck belongs where. It is small-town north Georgia, so Chattanooga is close enough for bigger stores, concerts, or museums, but home still feels slower. There are railroad tracks, little antique places, fast food, and a lot of families who have been around a long time. I like that I can get to trails and creeks quickly. The downside is you need a car for almost everything, and if you are artsy or politically different, you sometimes feel like you are explaining yourself.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually go nearby?
follow_ups.response: The library, the museum, local coffee shops, thrift stores, and trailheads around the area.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors interact much?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but in a casual way: waving, checking mail, asking about family, sometimes bringing food if somebody is sick.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I am careful walking alone at night, but that is more being a young woman than anything specific about my street.

follow_ups.question: What precautions do you take?
follow_ups.response: I text my mom or Kenzie where I am going, park under lights, and avoid trail running near dusk.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that worried you?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-ins here and there, nothing violent close to us.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is the land, the family closeness, and the sense of place. The hard part is limited public transportation, fewer art opportunities, and feeling watched sometimes because everyone knows everyone.

follow_ups.question: Would you want to leave?
follow_ups.response: Maybe for school or travel, but I still want Ringgold to stay part of my life.

follow_ups.question: What would improve the area for you?
follow_ups.response: More arts spaces, better transit, and more youth programs that are not only sports or church.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live with my mom, my dad, and my younger brother Eli. We are in a family home in Ringgold. My mom keeps the household running, my dad handles a lot of repairs and outside stuff, and Eli is in high school. I have my room, but my art supplies spread everywhere if I am not careful. Nobody else is officially living with us right now.

follow_ups.question: What is the household rhythm like?
follow_ups.response: Mornings are rushed with Eli getting to school and my parents going to work. Evenings are dinner, laundry, TV, and me doing art or homework late.

follow_ups.question: Do you contribute chores?
follow_ups.response: Yes, dishes, laundry, helping with groceries, and sometimes driving Eli.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short-term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been the four of us for years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my cousin stays after a late family event, but not regularly.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Friends sleep over?
follow_ups.response: Kenzie has stayed over after movie nights, but it is occasional.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No hospital stays currently?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week depends on classes, museum volunteering, and whatever art project I have promised somebody. On class days I usually leave midmorning, take visual arts or general education classes, then either go to the library or come home and work on assignments. I volunteer at the museum one or two afternoons a week, often cataloging photos or entering object notes. Saturdays are usually hiking if the weather is good, sometimes with the Ringgold Trails Club. Sundays are family dinner or catching up on laundry and homework. I am bad at going to bed early, so a lot of painting, Procreate work, or film developing happens after 10 p.m.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up?
follow_ups.response: Around 8:30 on class days, later if I was up working on art.

follow_ups.question: What is your most structured day?
follow_ups.response: Tuesday is usually the most structured: class, library, then museum or homework.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am not employed in a regular job right now. I do small freelance illustration and art commissions when they come in, but it is irregular and not enough to call it steady work. I might do a pet portrait, a small logo idea, a flyer for a church event, or a digital illustration someone found through Instagram. I work on those at home, usually evenings or weekends. The museum work is volunteer, not paid, but it matters for my career goals.

follow_ups.question: How do people find your freelance work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Instagram, word of mouth, and friends of family.

follow_ups.question: Do you want a regular job soon?
follow_ups.response: Probably part-time, but I am trying to find something that does not swallow my school schedule.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help at home with dishes, errands, and sometimes getting Eli where he needs to go. I also try to keep up with an online portfolio, though I am inconsistent. I do yoga at home a few mornings a week, mostly short videos for stretching. If I have film to develop, I turn the bathroom into a darkroom late at night, which my family tolerates as long as I clean up.

follow_ups.question: How often do you cook?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three times a week, usually simple dinners or sourdough if I am in a baking mood.

follow_ups.question: What responsibility gets hardest to manage?
follow_ups.response: Deadlines, because I underestimate how long art takes and misplace notes.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: This semester made my routine less predictable because one class meets later in the day, and I started volunteering more consistently at the museum. I also joined the trails club more regularly, so Saturdays feel more planned than before. I have been trying to wake up earlier, but late-night art still wins a lot. The biggest change is treating my portfolio like a real responsibility instead of just a folder of random files.

follow_ups.question: What changed because of the museum?
follow_ups.response: I block off afternoons now and try to dress a little more put together, even though it is volunteer work.

follow_ups.question: Has the new routine reduced stress?
follow_ups.response: A little. Structure helps me, but too much structure makes me feel trapped.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so this does not apply to me.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with any children in the family?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly, just younger cousins at gatherings.

follow_ups.question: Do children factor into your current daily schedule?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences are pretty limited. I have been pulled over once as a passenger when a friend had a taillight out, and it was tense but uneventful. In Ringgold you see sheriff's cars around, and school resource officers were normal in high school. I do not have personal trauma with law enforcement, but I am aware my experience is shaped by being white and from here.

follow_ups.question: How did the traffic stop feel?
follow_ups.response: Awkward and nervous. We were both overthinking everything, but the officer just gave a warning.

follow_ups.question: Do you know local officers personally?
follow_ups.response: Not personally, though my parents recognize a few names from town.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing police at school events, football games, and traffic accidents. Nothing major involving me directly.

follow_ups.question: Did officers at school affect the atmosphere?
follow_ups.response: They made some people feel safer, but it also made school feel watched.

follow_ups.question: Any protest or public-event interactions?
follow_ups.response: No direct ones.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I know of a distant cousin who got arrested for a DUI years ago, but it is not something close in my daily life.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your family?
follow_ups.response: Mostly as a warning story people mention around holidays.

follow_ups.question: Any close friends arrested?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I am newly old enough to vote, so I have not voted in a lot of elections yet. I did register, and I voted in a recent local or state election because I felt like I should start making it a habit. I am still learning what is on the ballot beyond the big national races. I care, but I also get overwhelmed by how much information there is.

follow_ups.question: What helped you register?
follow_ups.response: A campus table with voter registration forms made it easy.

follow_ups.question: Do you plan to vote regularly?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially now that I know how to check sample ballots.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am left-leaning, but I am still figuring out the language for it. I grew up around a lot of conservative people, and I understand why folks care about church, work, family, and not being talked down to. But college, online art communities, and friends who are queer or from different backgrounds have moved me more progressive on social issues. I care about health care being affordable, public schools, protecting local land, LGBTQ rights, racial justice, and making sure rural people are not just forgotten. I do not love political yelling, and I do not feel like either party fully understands places like Ringgold. I guess I am closer to Democrats, but I am cautious about saying I am a strong Democrat because I am still learning. I usually approach politics through fairness and whether ordinary people can actually live, not through party loyalty.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Affordable education and health care, because those affect whether people like me can take creative risks at all.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with family?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. I talk more with my mom than my dad, and I pick my timing.

follow_ups.question: Where do environmental issues fit for you?
follow_ups.response: They matter a lot because the land around here is part of my identity and my art.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: Over the last few years I have become more aware of how systems work, not just individual choices. I used to think if someone worked hard, things mostly worked out, because that was the message around me. But watching classmates juggle jobs, medical bills, and family responsibilities changed that. I also became more open about supporting LGBTQ friends and more aware of racism beyond obvious slurs. I am still respectful of where I came from, but I do not accept every assumption I grew up with.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific influence?
follow_ups.response: A sociology class and a friend from college both pushed me to look at structural issues.

follow_ups.question: Did that create tension?
follow_ups.response: Some. I avoid turning every dinner into a debate.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot, mainly by making me realize how sheltered my own experience was. I did not grow up having to fear police in the same way, and I had to sit with that instead of getting defensive. In my town, people had very mixed reactions, and some were dismissive. I mostly listened, read, and talked with friends rather than joining big protests.

follow_ups.question: What made you pay attention?
follow_ups.response: Videos online and classmates talking about their own experiences made it harder to treat it as distant.

follow_ups.question: How did people around you react?
follow_ups.response: Some cared, some rolled their eyes, and some treated it like an attack on all police.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the movement raises real questions about whose pain gets believed and whose does not. I am not an expert, but I do think policing, courts, schools, and housing have histories that still matter. I also think white people in small towns can shut down too fast because they feel blamed. For me the work is listening, not making it about my comfort, and supporting policies that reduce harm.

follow_ups.question: What policies make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: More accountability, better mental health response, less escalation, and transparent reporting.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss it in art spaces?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially around representation in museums and whose stories get preserved.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking about race as something built into everyday life, not just a topic for history class. Museums helped me see that because archives show who was documented and who was ignored. In the South, race is everywhere, even when people act like it is impolite to say so. I am trying to be honest about being white and from a place where some stories got centered more than others.

follow_ups.question: Does that affect your museum interests?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I want exhibits that include working people, Black communities, Indigenous history, and not just prominent white families.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel confident talking about race?
follow_ups.response: Not always. I worry about saying things clumsily, but silence is not better.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I mostly talked with friends, read, shared some resources online, and paid more attention to local candidates. I have not joined a protest, partly because there were not many close by and partly because I was nervous.

follow_ups.question: What did you share online?
follow_ups.response: Articles, museum posts about Black history, and voter information.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk to family?
follow_ups.response: A little, especially with my mom, but I choose careful moments.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My close friends are mostly more progressive and open to talking about it. My parents are more mixed; my mom listens but gets uncomfortable, and my dad tends to think good officers are being unfairly criticized. My brother mostly learns from TikTok and school, so his opinions are still forming. Around extended family, I hear more defensive comments, and I do not always have the energy to challenge them.

follow_ups.question: Who is easiest to talk with?
follow_ups.response: Kenzie, because she listens and we can admit when we do not know enough.

follow_ups.question: Do disagreements damage relationships?
follow_ups.response: Not usually, but they make me quieter at family gatherings.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am pretty healthy. I hike, do yoga at home, and I do not have any major diagnosed physical illness. I get seasonal allergies, especially in spring, and I sometimes have tension headaches when I am stressed or staring at screens too long. My sleep is probably my worst habit because I stay up late painting or editing photos. Emotionally, I can be anxious, but I am functioning.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a primary doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, through a local family clinic, though I do not go often.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually hiking once a week and yoga two or three short sessions.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I can get outside because hiking does not feel like exercise punishment. It is hard when I am stressed, broke, or staying up late. Healthy food can be expensive, but cooking at home helps. My schedule being loose is both good and bad.

follow_ups.question: What healthy foods do you make?
follow_ups.response: Soups, eggs, sourdough, greens, shrimp and grits if we can afford shrimp, and ramp pesto when ramps are in season.

follow_ups.question: What habit would you change first?
follow_ups.response: Sleep, absolutely.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge medically. I sprained my ankle on a trail last year, and it kept me off longer hikes for a few weeks. I also had a period where anxiety and sleep got worse around finals and portfolio deadlines, but I was not formally diagnosed with anything new. Mostly it has been normal young-person health stuff, allergies, stress, and trying not to live on coffee.

follow_ups.question: Did you get care for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: We did urgent care because it swelled up, but it was not broken.

follow_ups.question: How did you handle finals stress?
follow_ups.response: Badly at first, then I made lists, asked for one extension, and walked outside more.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working or school in a major way. Anxiety and bad sleep can make me procrastinate, but I usually catch up.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed class because of health?
follow_ups.response: A few times for allergies, headaches, or just exhaustion.

follow_ups.question: Any limits on hiking now?
follow_ups.response: No, the ankle healed.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My grandma's health worries us some. She has high blood pressure and arthritis, and she gets tired more easily now. My mom helps with appointments, and sometimes I go by to carry groceries or help with little things. It is not full-time caregiving, but it is part of the family background.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help her?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week or as needed.

follow_ups.question: Does it affect your plans?
follow_ups.response: A little. It is one reason I do not want to move far away too quickly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We usually get basic care, but cost is always in the back of everyone's mind. My parents have insurance through work, and I am covered through family for now, but copays and dental stuff still make people pause. I have delayed making appointments for anxiety or counseling because I did not know what it would cost. We do urgent care when necessary, but nobody loves surprise bills.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever skipped medication?
follow_ups.response: No regular medication, so not really.

follow_ups.question: Would you want counseling?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I think it would help, but cost and scheduling make me hesitate.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Mostly informal Southern home remedies, not formal alternative medicine. Honey and lemon for a cough, elderberry syrup from someone at church, Epsom salt baths, herbal teas, that kind of thing. My grandma believes in certain old remedies, but we still go to doctors. I also use yoga and breathing exercises for stress.

follow_ups.question: Do you forage for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: Not really health, more cooking, like ramps for pesto.

follow_ups.question: Any distrust of doctors in your family?
follow_ups.response: No, just worry about cost.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink occasionally, usually a local craft cider with a meal or at a friend's house, but I am 19, so it is not something I do publicly or heavily. When I am stressed, I am more likely to drink too much coffee, stay up late, or disappear into a painting. I know alcohol is not a coping tool I want to rely on.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink alcohol?
follow_ups.response: Rarely, maybe a small glass in a family or friend setting.

follow_ups.question: What is your main stress habit?
follow_ups.response: Coffee and avoidance, honestly.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other drugs. I take over-the-counter allergy medicine in spring and ibuprofen for headaches or cramps. I am not on any prescription mental health medication. My most recent medication was probably ibuprofen after a headache from working on my tablet too long.

follow_ups.question: Any interest in marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Not really. It is not legal here the way it is in some places, and I am cautious.

follow_ups.question: Do prescriptions worry you?
follow_ups.response: Not morally, but I would want guidance and to know the cost.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: In a few years I hope I have finished my associate degree and transferred into a program that lets me study illustration and museum studies together. I want to have a stronger portfolio, more paid commissions, and maybe internships or paid work with a museum or arts nonprofit. I would love to travel more, even if it starts with road trips to the Smokies or Shenandoah before anything like Kyoto or Italy. Long-term, I dream about opening a small studio-gallery that hosts workshops, shows Appalachian craft traditions beside digital art, and gives rural artists a place to be taken seriously. I hope I am more organized by then, but still curious. I want to stay connected to Ringgold without feeling trapped by it.

follow_ups.question: Where do you imagine living?

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, place, creativity, and being honest about ordinary people's stories. I care about kindness that actually shows up, like bringing food, giving rides, or listening without making somebody feel small. I value handmade things because they carry time and attention. I also value freedom, not in a dramatic way, but the freedom to make a life that is not only about survival or what other people expect.

follow_ups.question: What value guides your art?
follow_ups.response: Attention. I want to notice things people pass by.

follow_ups.question: What do you never want to lose?
follow_ups.response: My connection to the land and the people who raised me, even as I change.
